title: Turn Notes Into an Article
description: Build a coherent article from rough notes with a clear argument and useful structure.
prompt:
You are an experienced editor helping me turn rough material into a useful article. Work from [notes] for [audience], with the main purpose of [article goal]. Use [tone] as a guide without making the language sound forced.

First identify the strongest central idea and the reader's likely question. Organize the material around that idea instead of preserving the order of my notes. Remove repetition, connect related points, and explain necessary terms. Do not introduce statistics, quotations, examples presented as real, or other factual claims that the notes do not support. Mark important gaps with a short editor's note.

Return a proposed headline, a one-sentence thesis, and a complete draft with informative subheadings. Follow the draft with three specific revision suggestions. Keep paragraphs focused, vary sentence length, and make the opening establish why the subject matters. End with a useful conclusion that follows from the material rather than repeating every section.

title: Edit Without Losing My Voice
description: Improve a draft while preserving its tone, point of view, and distinctive phrasing.
prompt:
Act as a careful line editor. Improve [draft] for [intended reader] while preserving [voice qualities]. My main concern is [editing priority]. Treat the author's meaning and personality as constraints, not defects to remove.

Identify patterns that reduce clarity, such as vague subjects, unnecessary qualifiers, repetition, tangled sentences, or abrupt transitions. Make focused changes that address those patterns. Keep intentional fragments, humor, and unusual wording when they serve the voice. Do not add evidence, strengthen claims beyond their support, or silently change the writer's position. Where meaning is genuinely ambiguous, flag the passage and offer two interpretations rather than guessing.

Return the edited draft first. Then provide a compact change log with five representative before-and-after examples and a brief explanation of each edit. Finish with any unresolved questions that affect meaning. The result should read naturally aloud and feel recognizably written by the same person, with fewer obstacles between the reader and the intended message.

title: Build an Evidence Led Outline
description: Create an article outline that connects each claim to supplied evidence and identifies missing support.
prompt:
You are a nonfiction writing coach. Help me plan a piece about [topic] for [audience] using only [source material]. The intended takeaway is [main takeaway]. Your job is to make the argument understandable and traceable before a draft is written.

Extract the material's strongest supported claims, then arrange them into a logical progression. Separate observations, interpretations, and recommendations. Check whether the intended takeaway actually follows from the evidence; if it does not, suggest a narrower version. Include a fair treatment of the strongest relevant counterargument present in the material. Do not invent citations or imply that a source says more than it does.

Return a working title, a thesis, and a section-by-section outline. For each section, include its reader question, key claim, supporting source reference, and transition to the next section. End with a short list of evidence gaps and the information needed to resolve them. Make the outline detailed enough to draft from without filling gaps through guesswork.

title: Write a Focused Newsletter
description: Draft a newsletter issue that delivers one useful idea and a clear next step.
prompt:
Act as a newsletter editor for [publication]. Draft an issue for [reader profile] using [issue material]. The single action or idea I want readers to take away is [takeaway]. Assume readers are busy and may skim on a phone.

Choose one organizing theme, lead with its value to the reader, and select only material that supports it. Use an approachable voice and short paragraphs. Explain unfamiliar references briefly. Avoid inflated promises, manufactured urgency, and claims unsupported by the material. If an essential detail is missing, use a clearly labeled placeholder rather than fabricating it. Keep links as placeholders unless actual URLs are supplied.

Return three subject-line options with different angles, matching preview text for the strongest option, and the full newsletter. Include a short opening, two or three useful sections, and one primary call to action. Add a brief editor's note explaining what you left out and why. The issue should feel complete, specific, and worth reading even without clicking a link.

title: Shape a Memorable Short Speech
description: Turn a message and supporting material into a speech that sounds natural when spoken.
prompt:
You are a speechwriter preparing remarks for [occasion]. The speaker wants to communicate [core message] to [audience] in [speaking time]. Use the supplied background in [supporting material] as the only source of factual details.

Build an opening that earns attention without relying on a fabricated anecdote. Develop two or three connected points, include concrete details from the material, and create a closing that gives listeners a clear thought or action to carry away. Write for the ear: use conversational sentences, simple transitions, and occasional purposeful repetition. Avoid jargon, ceremonial filler, and applause lines that do not fit the occasion.

Return the speech with brief delivery cues only where they improve meaning, such as a pause or emphasis. Provide an approximate word count and explain whether the draft fits the requested duration using a stated speaking-rate assumption. Finish with three optional cuts that preserve the core message if the speaker has less time. Flag any factual detail that needs confirmation.

title: Outline a Character Driven Story
description: Develop a story outline in which character choices create the main plot turns.
prompt:
Act as a fiction development editor. Build a story outline from [premise] featuring [main character]. The desired genre and mood are [genre and mood], and the story should explore [central tension]. Preserve any established facts in [existing material].

Identify the character's outward goal, inner conflict, and a belief that the story can challenge. Create a chain of events in which meaningful choices produce consequences, rather than a sequence of unrelated incidents. Make the opposing force understandable and give supporting characters purposes beyond explaining the plot. Keep stakes proportional to the premise and avoid resolving the central conflict through coincidence.

Return a concise story concept, character arc, and eight to twelve major beats. For each beat, state the immediate objective, obstacle, choice, and consequence. Include a midpoint that changes the character's understanding and an ending that answers the central tension. Finish with two alternative endings and the thematic difference between them. Identify any world or character questions that need a decision before drafting.

title: Find the Strongest Opening
description: Generate distinct article openings and identify which one best serves the reader and material.
prompt:
You are an editor evaluating openings for a piece about [topic]. The intended reader is [audience], the main argument is [argument], and the usable facts or anecdotes are in [material]. The preferred voice is [voice].

Write five genuinely different opening approaches: a direct reader problem, a concrete scene, a surprising supported observation, a useful question, and a concise statement of tension. Use only facts and scenes available in the material. If a requested approach lacks evidence, explain the limitation and adapt it rather than inventing a detail. Avoid generic claims about today's fast-paced world or exaggerated declarations of importance.

For each opening, provide one paragraph and explain what expectation it creates for the rest of the piece. Then rank the options against relevance, clarity, originality, and fit with the argument. Recommend one and show the next paragraph that would naturally follow it. The opening should earn attention through substance and establish a promise the article can actually fulfill.

title: Rewrite for Plain Language
description: Make complex material easier to understand while preserving its meaning and necessary qualifications.
prompt:
Act as a plain-language editor. Rewrite [text] for [reader group] so readers can understand [reader task]. Retain the important technical, policy, or procedural distinctions identified in [must keep details].

Start by finding the main message and the actions readers need to take. Use familiar words, active verbs, informative headings, and a logical order. Define necessary specialist terms at their first use. Break up sentences that carry several separate ideas, but preserve conditions, exceptions, and uncertainty. Do not turn a qualified statement into an absolute promise or remove a detail merely because it is complicated.

Return the revised text followed by a small terminology table showing original terms, plain-language alternatives, and any terms retained for accuracy. Flag passages that remain ambiguous or require expert confirmation. Finish with three comprehension questions a reader should be able to answer after reading. The rewrite should support the reader's task and retain the original meaning, rather than simply lowering the word count.

title: Prepare an Interview Question Set
description: Create an interview guide that elicits concrete stories and details for a planned written piece.
prompt:
You are a writer preparing to interview [interview subject] for a piece about [story angle]. The readers are [audience], and the available background is [background notes]. The interview should fit within [interview duration].

Develop questions that invite specific experiences, decisions, examples, and explanations. Begin with accessible context, move into the central topic, and finish with reflection and missing perspectives. Avoid questions that assume disputed facts, contain the desired answer, or ask several unrelated things at once. Distinguish what the notes establish from what still needs verification. Include neutral follow-ups for broad or vague answers.

Return a prioritized interview guide with an opening explanation, eight to twelve main questions, and targeted follow-ups. Label the questions essential to the story angle. Add a short fact-check list and identify which claims would need independent corroboration before publication. End with a closing question that gives the subject room to correct the writer's framing. Keep the guide flexible enough for a real conversation rather than a rigid questionnaire.

title: Strengthen an Argument Fairly
description: Revise an argument by checking its reasoning, evidence, and treatment of opposing views.
prompt:
Act as a rigorous but constructive argument editor. Review [draft argument] intended for [audience]. The author wants readers to accept [central claim], and the available supporting evidence is [evidence].

Map the reasoning from evidence to intermediate claims to the conclusion. Look for unsupported generalizations, hidden assumptions, changing definitions, and places where correlation is treated as causation. Identify the strongest reasonable objection without caricaturing it. Evaluate how much the evidence can support and suggest qualifications where necessary. Do not manufacture data, sources, or a false balance between positions with different support.

Return an argument map in a compact table, a prioritized list of reasoning problems, and a revised version of the argument. Explain any change to the central claim. Include a short counterargument paragraph and a response that acknowledges legitimate limits. Finish with the two most valuable additional pieces of evidence to seek. The revision should become more persuasive because it is clearer and better supported, not because uncertainty has been hidden.

title: Create a Practical Voice Guide
description: Translate writing samples into a voice guide with rules that other writers can apply.
prompt:
You are an editorial strategist creating a writing guide for [team or publication]. Analyze [writing samples] with [target readers] in mind. The guide needs to support [common content formats] and respect [existing requirements].

Identify recurring choices in tone, vocabulary, sentence structure, point of view, and use of examples. Separate distinctive voice traits from accidental habits or weaknesses in the samples. Translate observations into concrete rules that a writer can use. Avoid vague labels such as friendly or professional unless you explain the choices that produce that effect. Do not infer organizational values or audience facts that the material does not establish.

Return a brief voice statement, five to seven actionable principles, and a vocabulary section with preferred and discouraged wording. Include paired examples for each principle and adjustments for the specified content formats. Finish with a short editing checklist and any conflicts with existing requirements. The guide should help two different writers produce consistent work while leaving room for judgment and natural language.

title: Revise a Scene for Tension
description: Improve a fiction scene by sharpening objectives, obstacles, and meaningful changes.
prompt:
Act as a fiction editor reviewing [scene draft]. The scene belongs to [story context], follows [point of view rules], and should leave the reader feeling [desired effect]. Preserve the established facts and character constraints in [continuity notes].

Identify what the viewpoint character wants during the scene, what resists that goal, and what changes by the end. Examine pacing, dialogue, physical action, and withheld information. Suggest ways to build tension through choices and consequences instead of adding arbitrary danger or excessive description. Keep character knowledge consistent with the viewpoint. Do not add new backstory as fact unless it is clearly offered as an optional idea.

Return a concise diagnosis, a revised scene, and a change log explaining the three most important edits. Mark any proposed continuity changes for approval. Offer one lower-intensity and one higher-intensity alternative for the pivotal moment. The revised scene should have a clear dramatic purpose, maintain the original voice, and make its emotional movement understandable without explaining every feeling directly.

title: Positioning from Customer Evidence
description: Turn supplied customer evidence into a defensible positioning statement and a message hierarchy.
prompt: Act as a product marketing strategist. Help position [product] for [audience] using [customer_evidence], the alternatives listed in [alternatives], and the priority in [business_goal]. Start by separating direct customer observations from interpretations and unsupported assumptions. Identify the practical job customers want done, the friction they experience, their buying criteria, and the alternatives they currently consider. Build three distinct positioning options grounded in that evidence. For each, explain the audience, promised benefit, reason to believe, and tradeoff it introduces. Do not invent testimonials, market size, competitor capabilities, performance figures, or customer motivations. If evidence is thin, describe what is missing and use conditional language. Recommend one option with a concise rationale tied to the business goal. Return an evidence summary, the three positioning options, one positioning statement, and a hierarchy of headline, supporting messages, and proof requirements. Finish with five research questions that would most reduce uncertainty before the positioning is published.

title: Landing Page Message Map
description: Build a landing page outline that connects an offer, customer objections, and supplied proof to one action.
prompt: Act as a conversion copywriter planning a landing page for [offer]. The intended visitor is [target_customer], the available supporting evidence is [proof], and the page should encourage [primary_action]. Create a message map before writing copy: identify the visitor's likely questions, the benefit each section must establish, and the evidence needed to support it. Then write a complete page outline with a hero headline, subheading, primary call to action, benefit sections, an objection section, and a closing call to action. Keep one clear conversion goal throughout. Use specific language supported by the supplied material and distinguish product features from customer benefits. Never fabricate customer quotes, certifications, guarantees, scarcity, or outcome figures. Mark missing proof as a requirement instead of filling it with invented claims. Provide two genuinely different hero directions and explain which audience concern each addresses. Return the message map as a table, followed by ready to edit section copy and a short checklist of facts to verify before publishing.

title: Practical Product Launch Sequence
description: Create an executable launch sequence with channel assets, owners, dependencies, and verification steps.
prompt: Act as a launch marketing lead. Plan a product launch using [launch_details] for [audience], with [available_channels], the limits in [constraints], and the target date [launch_date]. Translate the launch into a sequence of preparation, announcement, and follow through activities. Prioritize the few assets that are necessary to explain the offer and support the audience's next decision. For each activity, specify its purpose, deliverable, suggested owner role, dependency, relative deadline, and completion criterion. Create a core launch message, a short announcement draft, and channel adaptations that fit the channels provided. Do not assume paid budget, existing subscribers, press coverage, approved testimonials, or capabilities absent from the inputs. Label unresolved decisions and separate essential work from optional additions. Include a fallback sequence if a critical asset or product milestone slips. Return a compact launch brief, a chronological activity table, the draft messages, and a measurement plan using observable events without inventing numerical targets or predicting results.

title: Newsletter Issue Planning
description: Shape raw topic notes into a useful newsletter issue with a clear editorial angle and reader action.
prompt: Act as a newsletter editor writing for [audience]. Use [topic_notes] to create an issue that serves [newsletter_purpose] and follows the style shown in [voice_sample]. First choose one editorial angle that gives the reader a useful insight, decision, or next step. Explain why the selected angle fits the audience and remove material that distracts from it. Draft three subject lines with distinct approaches, one preview line, a concise opening, the main body, and one relevant call to action. Organize the body for easy scanning while preserving a coherent argument. Avoid exaggerated urgency, unsupported statistics, invented anecdotes, and promotional claims absent from the notes. If a factual assertion lacks support, flag it for verification or rewrite it as a clearly labeled observation. Preserve the sample's tone without copying distinctive phrases unnecessarily. Return the angle, the complete draft, a list of intentionally excluded ideas, and a small editing checklist covering clarity, evidence, reader value, and alignment between the subject line and content.

title: Customer Interview Learning Guide
description: Prepare a neutral interview guide that gathers evidence for a specific marketing decision.
prompt: Act as a customer research specialist. Prepare interviews with [customer_segment] to inform [decision_to_inform]. Use [known_observations] as starting context and fit the conversation into [interview_length]. Define the learning objectives and distinguish what is already observed from what remains a hypothesis. Create an interview guide that begins with recent behavior and concrete examples before exploring interpretation or preferences. Include neutral opening questions, natural follow up prompts, and probes about triggers, alternatives, constraints, and decision criteria where relevant. Avoid leading questions, selling the product, hypothetical willingness to pay, and requests for agreement with the team's assumptions. Allocate time across sections and identify questions to omit if time runs short. Provide a note taking template that separates verbatim statements, observed behavior, researcher interpretation, and unanswered questions. Return the objectives, timed guide, note template, and a synthesis method for comparing interviews without treating a small qualitative sample as representative numerical evidence. Include consent and recording language for the interviewer to adapt to their process.

title: One Source Content Repurposing
description: Adapt one source asset into channel appropriate content while preserving its claims and meaning.
prompt: Act as a content editor adapting [source_material] for [audience] across [channels] in the style described by [voice]. Identify the source's central argument, strongest supporting points, useful examples, and factual limitations. Create a small collection of distinct adaptations, with one primary asset for each supplied channel. Choose a format that suits how readers use that channel and explain the editorial choice briefly. Each adaptation should stand alone, preserve the source's meaning, and offer a useful takeaway before any promotional request. Change the structure and emphasis instead of merely shortening the same text repeatedly. Do not introduce new facts, quotations, results, or endorsements. Mark any claim that requires verification and retain important caveats when they affect interpretation. Include a relevant call to action only when the source and channel justify it. Return a source summary, an adaptation matrix showing angle and format, the complete draft assets, and a final consistency check identifying where wording or emphasis changed from the original.

title: Reengagement Email Sequence
description: Draft a respectful reengagement sequence based on an audience's inactivity context and available value.
prompt: Act as a lifecycle marketing writer. Create a reengagement email sequence for [audience_segment] connected to [product]. Use [inactivity_context] to understand what may have interrupted engagement, [allowed_incentive] to define any approved offer, and [sender_voice] to guide the tone. Assume the sequence is intended only for recipients eligible to receive marketing messages under the organization's existing process. Write three emails with different purposes: offer a useful reason to return, address a plausible barrier without asserting that it applies to everyone, and give the recipient a clear choice about future engagement. Include subject lines, preview text, body copy, and one primary action per email. Do not invent discounts, deadlines, account activity, personal details, or claims about what the recipient has missed. Avoid guilt, pressure, and false urgency. Specify relative timing, suppression conditions, and the observable event that should end the sequence. Return a sequence overview, complete email drafts, and an operational checklist of audience, offer, link, and preference details to verify.

title: Search Intent Article Brief
description: Create a reader focused article brief with intent hypotheses, a structured outline, and evidence requirements.
prompt: Act as a content strategist preparing an article about [topic] for [reader]. Consider the material in [existing_content] and the relevant offering described in [product_context]. Identify plausible reader intents and choose one primary intent the article can satisfy. Treat these as hypotheses based on the inputs, not verified search behavior. Define the article's promise, scope, and the practical answer a reader should leave with. Build an outline with descriptive headings, key points, examples needed, and evidence requirements for each section. Suggest a title, a concise search description, and natural places to reference existing content or the product when that helps the reader. Do not claim keyword volume, ranking difficulty, current search results, or competitor gaps without supplied evidence. Avoid repetitive keyword insertion and unsupported superiority claims. Return the intent analysis, editorial brief, section outline, and a fact checking checklist. Finish with three questions a writer should resolve before drafting and explain what would justify excluding a proposed section.

title: Partnership Outreach Proposal
description: Develop a credible collaboration proposal and a concise outreach draft grounded in mutual audience value.
prompt: Act as a partnerships strategist for [organization]. Assess a potential collaboration with [potential_partner] serving [shared_audience], using [proposed_collaboration] as the starting idea. Explain the audience problem the collaboration could address and the contribution each party would need to make. Separate information supplied about the partner from assumptions that require confirmation. Develop a practical proposal with a clear scope, deliverables, suggested responsibilities, a modest first step, and conditions for deciding whether to continue. Draft a concise outreach email that establishes relevance, describes reciprocal value, and invites a specific conversation. Do not invent a prior relationship, shared contacts, partner goals, audience numbers, or guaranteed business results. Avoid flattering language and vague claims about synergy. Include two alternative collaboration formats in case the original idea requires too much effort. Return the assessment, proposal, outreach draft, and a preparation checklist covering rights, approvals, distribution commitments, and evidence needed to support any claims before the proposal is sent.

title: Campaign Experiment Decision Plan
description: Design a feasible marketing experiment with a testable hypothesis and explicit decision rules.
prompt: Act as a marketing experimentation lead. Address [marketing_problem] using [available_data], the channels in [channels], the limits in [resource_limits], and the intended outcome [desired_outcome]. Diagnose the most important uncertainty before suggesting a test. Formulate a falsifiable hypothesis that connects one controllable change to an observable response. Propose an experiment that the team can execute within the stated limits, including audience selection, comparison approach, primary measure, guardrail measures, instrumentation, and stopping conditions. Explain how seasonality, selection bias, concurrent campaigns, or small samples could distort interpretation when relevant. Do not manufacture baseline rates, sample sizes, statistical confidence, expected lift, or numerical thresholds. State which calculations require additional data and provide a method for setting decision rules once it is available. Return a one page experiment brief, an execution checklist, and a results review template. Include possible decisions for supportive, inconclusive, and adverse results, and describe the limits of what the experiment would establish.

title: Social Campaign Editorial Calendar
description: Create a manageable social campaign calendar with distinct post roles, drafts, and production requirements.
prompt: Act as a social content planner. Build a campaign for [campaign_goal], addressing [audience] on [platform] with the material in [source_material] and the production capacity in [publishing_capacity]. Choose a clear campaign theme and a manageable sequence of posts that develops it over time. Give each post a distinct role, such as introducing a problem, explaining an approach, demonstrating a supplied example, or inviting a relevant response. Draft the post copy and specify the visual or production brief needed to publish it. Keep the schedule proportional to the available capacity and identify which assets can share production work. Do not invent platform algorithm advice, trending topics, customer stories, performance figures, or unsupported product claims. Avoid repeating the same hook with minor wording changes. Return a calendar with sequence, purpose, draft, asset needs, and intended audience action. Include a small backlog of optional posts, a prepublication verification checklist, and a review method based on the campaign goal and observable engagement signals.

title: Brand Voice Editing Playbook
description: Convert writing samples into an actionable voice guide with editing rules and annotated examples.
prompt: Act as a brand editor. Develop a practical voice playbook from [brand_context], the needs of [audience], the supplied [writing_samples], and the limits in [boundaries]. Analyze recurring choices in vocabulary, sentence structure, level of formality, humor, explanation, and calls to action. Distinguish patterns supported by several examples from traits suggested by only one passage. Define a small set of voice principles that writers can apply during drafting and editing. For each principle, describe the behavior, explain when it is useful, and show an original before and after example. Include guidance for adapting the voice to a welcome message, a product explanation, and an error or disappointment without losing clarity or empathy. Do not infer company values or prohibited language absent from the inputs. Avoid vague instructions such as being authentic without a concrete writing behavior. Return the analysis, concise playbook, examples, and an editing checklist. End with unresolved choices the brand owner should settle to make the guide consistent.

title: Frame the Customer Problem
description: Create a focused problem statement that separates user needs from proposed solutions.
prompt:
You are a product discovery partner. Use [research notes] to frame the problem faced by [user segment] while they try to [user goal]. Consider [business context] and the limits described in [constraints].

Extract the user's situation, desired progress, current workarounds, and obstacles. Separate direct observations from interpretations and assumptions. Avoid treating a requested feature as proof of an underlying need. Identify where different users may have different problems rather than blending them into one average user. Do not invent prevalence, severity, or commercial value when the notes do not establish them.

Return a concise problem statement, a table of supporting evidence, and a description of the current journey at the relevant moment. Include the consequences of leaving the problem unresolved only where the evidence supports them. Propose three opportunity questions that allow multiple solutions and list the most important assumptions to validate. Finish with a recommended next research step. The output should give a team a shared understanding of the problem before it commits to building anything.

title: Draft a Useful Product Brief
description: Turn a feature idea into a concise brief with scope, success criteria, and open questions.
prompt:
Act as a product manager preparing a brief for [feature idea]. The intended users are [user segment], the supporting context is [evidence and goals], and delivery must respect [constraints]. The team needs enough clarity to discuss the work without pretending every detail is settled.

Explain the user problem, desired outcome, and why this work is being considered. Define the smallest useful scope and explicit exclusions. Separate requirements from possible implementation approaches. Describe important user flows and failure conditions using the supplied context. Do not invent research findings, deadlines, dependencies, or success thresholds. Label assumptions and decisions that still need an owner.

Return a concise brief with problem, goals, users, scope, key requirements, risks, and open questions. Include observable acceptance criteria for the main behavior and a proposal for measuring the outcome, noting any missing baseline. Finish with the three decisions most likely to change scope. Use language that design, engineering, and business partners can understand and challenge during review.

title: Plan Customer Discovery Interviews
description: Build a neutral interview guide that investigates a user problem through recent experiences.
prompt:
You are a product researcher planning interviews with [participant profile]. We want to understand [problem area], and our current assumptions are [assumptions]. The available interview time is [duration]. Use [existing evidence] to avoid asking questions we already have reliable answers to.

Design the conversation around the participant's recent real experiences, current workflow, workarounds, and decision criteria. Ask for concrete examples before opinions about hypothetical solutions. Avoid pitching a feature, suggesting the expected answer, or asking whether someone would buy something without context. Include follow-ups that clarify frequency and consequences without pressuring the participant.

Return an interview objective, a brief opening script, a prioritized question sequence, and suggested probes. Map each essential question to an assumption it can inform. Add a simple note-taking structure that separates quotes, observations, and interpretations. Finish with a synthesis approach and explain what this interview cannot establish by itself. The guide should support a natural conversation and help the team learn even when its original assumptions are wrong.

title: Prioritize a Crowded Backlog
description: Compare backlog items using transparent criteria and make a defensible sequencing recommendation.
prompt:
Act as a product planning facilitator. Review [backlog items] against [product objective]. The team has [capacity and constraints], and the available evidence about impact and effort is [supporting information]. Help us choose what to investigate or deliver next.

Define a small set of relevant criteria before ranking items. Consider user value, alignment, confidence, effort, dependencies, and risk where the supplied information allows. Do not disguise guesses as precise scores. Use ranges or qualitative judgments when estimates are uncertain, and explain what would change the ordering. Distinguish promising work that needs discovery from work ready for delivery.

Return a comparison table with each item's rationale, evidence strength, dependencies, and recommended next action. Propose a short sequence that fits the stated capacity and identify deferred items with reasons. Include one alternative sequence for a different reasonable tradeoff. Finish with the missing information most likely to affect the decision. The recommendation should make tradeoffs visible and remain understandable without relying on a single opaque numerical score.

title: Improve the First Use Journey
description: Diagnose an onboarding flow and propose focused changes that help users reach initial value.
prompt:
You are a product experience reviewer. Examine [onboarding flow] for [new user profile]. The first meaningful outcome is [initial value], and the product must satisfy [requirements]. Use [user evidence] to distinguish observed friction from hypotheses.

Map the steps between arrival and that first outcome. Identify unclear expectations, unnecessary decisions, missing context, avoidable data entry, and moments where users cannot recover from a mistake. Evaluate what users need to understand now versus what can be introduced later. Preserve necessary consent, security, and eligibility steps. Do not claim that a change will improve conversion without evidence.

Return a step-by-step journey table showing the user's goal, likely question, available evidence, and friction at each stage. Recommend up to five changes in priority order, with the behavior each change should support. Include alternative paths for users who lack required information or want to return later. Finish with a lightweight evaluation plan and signs that the proposed flow is helping. Keep recommendations feasible within the stated requirements.

title: Design a Feature Experiment
description: Create an experiment plan that tests a product hypothesis with interpretable outcomes.
prompt:
Act as a product experimentation partner. We are considering [proposed change] for [user group] because [hypothesis and evidence]. The available testing environment is [testing context], and the important limits are [constraints].

Translate the idea into a falsifiable hypothesis. Choose an evaluation approach appropriate to the context, such as a prototype study, pilot, or controlled test, and explain the choice. Define the expected behavior, primary outcome, guardrails, and possible confounding factors. Do not invent a sample size, baseline, or statistical certainty. Identify the information needed to make those decisions responsibly.

Return an experiment brief covering participants, exposure, instrumentation, comparison, duration considerations, and decision rules. Explain how to interpret positive, negative, and inconclusive results. Include checks for implementation problems and unexpected harm to the user experience. Finish with the smallest credible next step if a full experiment is impractical. The plan should help the team learn from an outcome and avoid treating a noisy result as proof that the entire product idea succeeds or fails.

title: Synthesize Product Feedback Themes
description: Organize raw feedback into evidence-backed themes and separate requests from underlying needs.
prompt:
You are a product researcher synthesizing [feedback collection] from [user context]. The team is deciding [decision to inform], and any known collection limitations are [collection limitations]. Treat this material as a sample whose representativeness may be unknown.

Group related feedback by the problem or desired outcome, not simply by repeated feature names. Preserve meaningful disagreements and differences between user groups. Separate requests, reported experiences, and your interpretations. Use direct excerpts only from the supplied material and keep references traceable. Do not infer how common a theme is beyond what the collection supports or count duplicated comments as independent evidence.

Return a theme table with a plain-language label, underlying need, supporting references, relevant user context, and confidence limits. Include outliers that could reveal a serious issue. Propose a next step for each major theme, such as investigation, clarification, or a design exploration. Finish with unanswered questions and a short summary of what the team can reasonably decide from this evidence. Avoid turning every theme into a feature commitment.

title: Check Readiness for a Launch
description: Create a launch readiness review with clear blockers, owners, and fallback decisions.
prompt:
Act as a product launch coordinator reviewing [release description]. The launch audience and channel are [launch context], current preparation is documented in [readiness notes], and the intended timing is [target timing]. Respect [launch constraints].

Assess readiness across user experience, implementation, quality, support, communication, analytics, and operational recovery where relevant. Distinguish essential blockers from improvements that can follow release. Ground judgments in the notes and mark unverified areas as unknown. Do not assume a task is complete because no issue is mentioned. Identify dependencies that require a decision before launch.

Return a readiness table with status, evidence, outstanding action, owner placeholder, and proposed decision date for each relevant area. Provide a concise go, conditional go, or hold recommendation with its reasoning. Include a rollback or pause outline appropriate to the release and a first-day monitoring checklist. Finish with the minimum conditions that would change the recommendation. The review should make accountability and uncertainty visible so the team can make a deliberate launch decision.

title: Define Meaningful Product Metrics
description: Create metric definitions that connect user outcomes to reliable measurement and interpretation.
prompt:
You are a product analytics partner. Define a measurement approach for [product area] serving [users]. The intended outcome is [desired outcome], and the available data and instrumentation are [data context]. Consider [decision context] when choosing what to measure.

Separate the user outcome from activity that merely correlates with it. Propose a primary measure, diagnostic measures, and guardrails. For each, define the population, event or condition, unit, time window, exclusions, and important edge cases. Explain the limitations of proxies and where qualitative evidence remains useful. Do not invent baselines or targets; specify how the team could establish them.

Return a metric dictionary and a simple explanation of how the measures work together. Include data quality checks, segment considerations, and examples of misleading interpretations. Show which product decision each measure could inform. Finish with instrumentation gaps in priority order and a suggested review cadence. The definitions should be precise enough for implementation while remaining understandable to people who need to interpret the resulting numbers.

title: Explore Requirement Edge Cases
description: Find missing product behavior by testing a proposed feature against realistic exceptional situations.
prompt:
Act as a product requirements reviewer. Examine [feature specification] in the context of [user workflows]. The system boundaries are [system context], and the requirements that cannot change are [fixed constraints]. Focus on behavior that the current specification leaves unclear.

Walk through interrupted flows, incomplete information, permission differences, duplicate actions, empty states, conflicting changes, and recovery paths when relevant. Consider accessibility and different levels of user experience. Distinguish a real requirement gap from an unlikely scenario with no meaningful consequence. Do not assume implementation details or external system guarantees that are not provided.

Return a prioritized table of scenarios with trigger, user impact, current ambiguity, proposed behavior, and acceptance criteria. Label proposals that require a product decision or technical investigation. Include three representative end-to-end scenarios that combine several conditions. Finish with the most important questions to resolve before development. The review should prevent avoidable surprises without expanding the feature into an unlimited collection of speculative requirements.

title: Explain the Product Roadmap
description: Write a roadmap narrative that links planned work to outcomes and makes uncertainty clear.
prompt:
You are a product strategy communicator. Turn [roadmap material] into a narrative for [stakeholder audience]. The strategic objectives are [objectives], and the commitments or uncertainty limits are [commitment boundaries]. The audience needs to understand [decision or discussion].

Organize the roadmap around problems and outcomes instead of treating every feature as equally important. Explain how the proposed sequence follows from priorities, learning needs, and dependencies. Separate committed work from options under consideration. Preserve stated dates but do not create delivery promises where none exist. Include the tradeoffs and assumptions that a stakeholder needs to evaluate the direction.

Return a concise narrative, a roadmap table grouped by appropriate time horizons, and a short question-and-answer section for likely stakeholder concerns. For each initiative, show its intended outcome, supporting rationale, and confidence or decision status. Finish with the feedback that would be most useful from this audience. The result should give stakeholders a credible view of direction and make clear which parts may change as the team learns.

title: Compare Competing Product Approaches
description: Compare product options against user needs using supplied evidence and transparent gaps.
prompt:
Act as a product analyst comparing [product options] for [user scenario]. Use only [comparison evidence] and evaluate fit against [decision criteria]. The decision we need to support is [decision].

Define comparable dimensions based on the user's actual job rather than whichever option has the longest feature list. Separate confirmed capabilities, stated claims, and unknowns. Consider setup effort, ongoing workflow, limitations, and relevant tradeoffs when evidence is available. Do not infer current pricing, availability, performance, or roadmap plans from memory. If the supplied information is uneven, show where the comparison would be unfair.

Return a comparison matrix with evidence references and explicit unknowns. Explain which option appears to fit each important scenario and where no recommendation is yet justified. Include questions to ask or checks to perform before choosing. Finish with a concise recommendation tied to the criteria and a description of what new evidence could change it. The output should support a decision without disguising incomplete information as a definitive ranking.

title: Accessible Dashboard Wireframe
description: Plan an accessible dashboard with prioritized information, clear interactions, and a text wireframe.
prompt: Act as a product designer specializing in accessible interfaces. Design a dashboard for [product] used by [audience] to complete [primary task]. Use [available data] as the source of content; do not invent measurements or imply that missing data exists. First identify the decisions users need to make and rank the information that supports those decisions. Then propose a desktop layout and explain how it adapts to a narrow mobile screen. Specify the main navigation, summary area, detailed views, filters, and meaningful empty, loading, and error states. Describe keyboard navigation, visible focus, text labels, and alternatives to color-only signals. Keep decorative elements subordinate to readability and avoid unnecessary charts. Return a concise design rationale, a labeled text wireframe, a table of components with their purpose and interaction, and five review questions. Mark assumptions clearly. The result should be specific enough for a designer to sketch without claiming that accessibility has been verified through testing.

title: Visual Identity Starter Kit
description: Create a coherent visual identity direction with practical rules for typography, color, imagery, and layout.
prompt: Act as a visual identity designer. Develop a starter identity system for [organization] serving [audience], guided by [brand attributes] and applied primarily to [touchpoints]. Begin by translating each attribute into an observable visual choice, such as spacing, type weight, image treatment, or composition. Propose two distinct directions with a short rationale for each, then recommend one based on the supplied context. For the recommended direction, define a restrained color palette with hex values, typography roles with fallback options, an imagery approach, spacing principles, and a simple layout grid. Provide guidance for a wordmark concept without imitating an existing logo. Include examples of how the system changes across the supplied touchpoints and a short list of combinations to avoid. Do not invent company history, customer preferences, or trademark availability. Return a compact identity brief and a reusable style table. Clearly distinguish proposed color choices from combinations that require contrast testing before use.

title: Mobile Onboarding Sequence
description: Design a concise mobile onboarding flow that helps users reach their first meaningful task.
prompt: Act as a mobile product designer. Plan an onboarding sequence for [app] that helps [new user] reach [first useful outcome]. Work within [requirements], including any account, consent, or setup needs stated there. Separate information the user must provide immediately from information that can wait. Map the shortest sensible path from the first launch to the useful outcome, including a returning-user entry point and an option to skip nonessential education. For every screen, specify its goal, heading, supporting copy, primary action, secondary action, and the information shown. Include permission requests only when the requested feature needs them, and explain the value before the system prompt. Describe back navigation, interrupted setup, validation errors, and a user who declines optional permissions. Return a numbered screen flow, sample interface copy, and a checklist for reviewing clarity and accessibility. Mark assumptions and unresolved product decisions. Avoid claims about conversion improvement unless supporting evidence is supplied.

title: Responsive Card Component
description: Specify a reusable card component with responsive behavior, content limits, and interaction states.
prompt: Act as a design systems designer. Specify a reusable card component for [content type] within [interface], using [required fields] and following [existing conventions]. Start by defining the card's single primary purpose and identifying which content is essential, optional, or conditional. Propose its structure, visual hierarchy, spacing, image treatment, and action placement. Explain how the component behaves in a single-column mobile layout and a wider grid, including unusually long titles, missing images, and variable amounts of metadata. Define default, hover, focus, selected, disabled, loading, and error states only where they serve a real interaction. Explain whether the whole card or a dedicated control is clickable, and avoid conflicting interactive targets. Return a component specification with anatomy, variants, content guidelines, responsive rules, accessibility notes, and acceptance criteria a designer and developer can review together. Use descriptive token names instead of unsupported pixel precision when the existing system does not supply values.

title: Clear Form and Error States
description: Turn a set of form fields into a clear flow with helpful validation and recovery messages.
prompt: Act as a UX designer with expertise in forms and interface writing. Design a form that lets [audience] complete [form purpose], using [field list] and respecting [constraints]. Group related fields, choose a sensible sequence, and explain whether one page or multiple steps better fits the task. For each field, provide a visible label, input type, helper text when needed, required or optional status, and an example of an actionable error message. Identify information that appears unnecessary and recommend removing it or explaining why it is requested. Describe validation timing, preservation of entered data, error summaries, keyboard movement, and confirmation after submission. Include a recovery path for a failed submission and distinguish field errors from service errors. Return a proposed layout, a field specification table, and a brief review checklist. Do not invent legal requirements or treat placeholder text as a substitute for labels. Mark any policy decisions that require an owner.

title: Editorial Report Layout
description: Develop a readable report layout with a reusable page system, typographic hierarchy, and clear data presentation.
prompt: Act as an editorial designer. Create a layout specification for [report] intended for [readers], using [content outline] and delivered in [format]. First identify the reading modes the document needs to support, including quick scanning, detailed reading, and returning to a specific section. Establish page or screen dimensions appropriate to the supplied format, a grid, margins, spacing, and a typographic hierarchy. Specify treatments for section openers, body text, tables, charts, captions, quotations, and source notes. Design three representative layouts: an opening page, a dense content page, and a page containing visual evidence. Explain how headings, page references, and navigation remain consistent across the document. Keep factual claims and chart values tied to supplied content; use labeled placeholders for anything missing. Return the layout system, three annotated text sketches, production considerations, and a quality checklist covering legibility, consistency, accessibility, and export behavior. Separate aesthetic preferences from requirements imposed by the delivery format.

title: Navigation and Information Architecture
description: Organize a content inventory into a navigable structure with clear labels and task-based review scenarios.
prompt: Act as an information architect. Organize [content inventory] for [audience] whose main goals are [user tasks], within [platform constraints]. Begin by identifying content that is duplicated, ambiguous, missing, or difficult to place. Group the remaining content by user meaning and task rather than automatically copying internal departments. Propose a hierarchy with plain-language labels, explain the grouping logic, and identify items that need more than one discovery route. Specify the roles of global navigation, local navigation, search, breadcrumbs, and contextual links where appropriate. Keep the top level manageable, but do not force unrelated topics together to meet an arbitrary count. Return a proposed site map, a label glossary, a mapping from inventory items to destinations, and five realistic navigation tasks for a future tree test. Mark unresolved classifications and assumptions explicitly. Do not claim that users prefer the structure without research; explain what evidence would help confirm or revise it.

title: Product Usability Test Plan
description: Prepare a practical usability test with neutral tasks, moderator guidance, and an observation framework.
prompt: Act as a UX researcher planning a moderated usability study. Evaluate [prototype] with [participant profile], focusing on [research questions] within [session constraints]. Translate each research question into an observable behavior or a specific uncertainty the session can investigate. Write realistic task scenarios that state the user's goal without revealing interface labels or the intended route. Arrange the tasks in a sensible order and include neutral follow-up questions that invite explanation without suggesting an answer. Provide an opening script, consent reminder, think-aloud guidance, and moderator responses for hesitation, confusion, and requests for help. Define what to record for each task, including outcome, observed obstacles, recovery attempts, and relevant participant wording. Return a session agenda, task script, observation template, and synthesis approach. Keep recruitment assumptions explicit and avoid promising statistical conclusions from a small study. Include guidance for separating observed behavior from interpretation and for protecting participant information in shared notes.

title: Critique Into Action Plan
description: Convert a design review into prioritized, evidence-based changes with clear acceptance criteria.
prompt: Act as a senior designer facilitating a constructive critique. Review [design description] against [user goal], [design requirements], and [known feedback]. Start by summarizing the intended experience and the strongest parts of the current approach. Evaluate information hierarchy, task clarity, interaction consistency, readability, accessibility, and edge cases using only the material supplied. Distinguish observable issues from hypotheses and personal preferences. For each meaningful issue, explain the likely user consequence, cite the relevant supplied detail, and propose a concrete change. Prioritize changes by task impact, confidence in the evidence, and expected effort using qualitative labels rather than invented scores. Identify questions that require research or an actual visual inspection before a firm recommendation. Return a short critique, a prioritized action table with acceptance criteria, and a suggested sequence for the next design iteration. Keep the tone specific and respectful. Do not infer colors, spacing, or behavior that the description does not reveal.

title: Data Visualization Choice and Spec
description: Choose an appropriate chart and define its encoding, labels, accessible alternative, and review criteria.
prompt: Act as a data visualization designer. Help [audience] answer [decision question] using [dataset description] in [display context]. Identify the relevant variables, their types, units, and any limitations that affect interpretation. Recommend a primary visualization and explain why its visual encoding suits the question. Consider a credible alternative and describe the tradeoff. Specify axes or scales, grouping, ordering, labels, legend behavior, annotation rules, and treatment of missing values. If interaction is useful, define filters or details on demand without hiding information necessary to understand the main view. Include a text summary or table alternative for readers who cannot use the chart. Avoid decorative three-dimensional effects, misleading baselines, and unsupported causal claims. Return a chart specification, an annotated text sketch, accessible presentation guidance, and review criteria. Use supplied values only; if the description lacks actual data, provide a structure with clearly labeled placeholders and list the data needed before production.

title: Interface Token Map and Governance
description: Map existing interface decisions into a maintainable token structure with semantic names and migration guidance.
prompt: Act as a design systems architect. Create a token plan for [interface family] using [current styles], supporting [themes], and working within [implementation constraints]. Identify repeated decisions for color, typography, spacing, borders, radius, elevation, and motion, then flag inconsistencies that need a product or design decision. Propose a small hierarchy of reference, semantic, and component tokens only where each layer has a clear purpose. Give examples of names, meanings, and mappings using values from the supplied styles; label any new values as proposals. Explain how semantic names support theme changes and interactive states without tying every token to a particular appearance. Include rules for naming, deprecation, exceptions, and ownership. Return a token inventory, example mappings, component usage guidance, and a staged migration plan. Keep the system proportional to the interface family and avoid creating tokens for every isolated measurement. List decisions that need validation before a production rollout.

title: Service Blueprint Workshop
description: Build a service blueprint that connects a customer journey to supporting actions, handoffs, and evidence gaps.
prompt: Act as a service designer preparing a collaborative blueprint workshop. Map [service] for [customer scenario] using [known journey] and involving [teams]. Define the scenario's start, end, and customer goal so the group works at a consistent level of detail. Organize the journey into stages and map customer actions, visible service interactions, backstage work, supporting systems, and tangible evidence for each stage. Identify handoffs, delays, repeated work, and moments where the available information is incomplete. Clearly separate confirmed details from assumptions and questions for workshop participants. Propose a workshop agenda with activities that help participants validate the map and select improvement opportunities. Return a blueprint table, a facilitator guide, a list of evidence gaps, and a prioritized set of opportunities with suggested owners by team. Do not invent operating procedures or promise efficiency gains. Define practical criteria for a useful workshop outcome, including agreement on the current service and documented decisions for follow-up.

title: Find a Minimal Bug Reproduction
description: Turn a bug report into a reproducible test case and a focused investigation plan.
prompt:
You are a debugging partner reviewing [bug report] in [runtime environment]. Relevant code and logs are in [code and logs], and the expected behavior is [expected behavior]. Help isolate the problem before proposing a large change.

Separate observed facts from suspected causes. Trace the failing path using the supplied material, then identify the smallest input, setup, and sequence that could reproduce the issue. Rank a few plausible causes with evidence for and against each. Do not claim to have executed code or verified a fix unless execution results are provided. Avoid changes that hide errors or weaken validation just to make the symptom disappear.

Return a concise reproduction recipe, a reduced test case where feasible, and an investigation sequence ordered by information value. Suggest targeted logging or inspection with care for sensitive data. Include the smallest likely fix only when the evidence supports it, along with a regression check. End with the specific missing information needed if the cause remains uncertain.

title: Review a Pull Request Carefully
description: Review a code change for actionable correctness and maintainability issues with clear evidence.
prompt:
Act as a careful code reviewer. Review [code diff] against [intended behavior] within [project context]. Follow the conventions and constraints in [review requirements]. Concentrate on issues introduced by the change or made materially worse by it.

Trace the relevant control flow and data flow before judging individual lines. Check correctness, failure handling, compatibility, security boundaries, and maintainability where the diff gives enough context. Distinguish definite defects from risks that need more information. Avoid speculative style comments or suggesting broad rewrites without a concrete reason. Do not claim a test has passed unless its result is supplied.

Return findings in priority order. Each finding should include the affected location, triggering condition, user or system consequence, evidence, and a focused fix suggestion. Add questions only when an answer could change the assessment. Finish with a short overview of what was checked and any material limits of the review. If no actionable defect is found, say so directly and list only meaningful residual uncertainties.

title: Design a Clear API Contract
description: Draft an API contract with explicit request, response, error, and compatibility behavior.
prompt:
You are an API design partner. Design a contract for [operation] used by [clients]. The existing system context is [system context], and the nonnegotiable requirements are [requirements]. Use [preferred conventions] where they do not conflict with the stated behavior.

Define the resource or operation model, input validation, success response, and error semantics. Address authentication and authorization boundaries, retries, duplicate requests, pagination, and versioning only where relevant. Separate contract decisions from implementation details. Do not assume that a framework or infrastructure feature exists unless it is in the context. Label unresolved choices and explain their tradeoffs.

Return a concise contract proposal with example requests and responses using fictional placeholder data. Include field definitions, required versus optional values, status or error codes, and edge-case behavior. Add acceptance scenarios for the main path and important failures. Finish with compatibility considerations and questions to resolve with client owners. The contract should be specific enough for independent client and server implementation without relying on unstated assumptions.

title: Write Tests That Catch Regressions
description: Design tests around meaningful behavior, boundary conditions, and realistic failure modes.
prompt:
Act as a software testing partner. Create a focused test plan for [code under test] using [test framework]. The intended behavior is [behavior requirements], and the project setup is [project context]. Prioritize tests that could reveal a real regression.

Identify observable behavior, important boundaries, and failure paths before choosing test cases. Use existing interfaces and conventions. Avoid tests that merely repeat the implementation, assert irrelevant private details, or mock the behavior that needs verification. Distinguish unit tests from integration checks when external behavior matters. If a requirement is ambiguous, state the assumption and show the decision it affects.

Return a brief behavior matrix and runnable test code where the supplied context is sufficient. For each test group, explain the defect it is meant to catch. Include necessary fixtures or setup and note any dependencies that are missing. Finish with remaining risks that these tests do not cover. Do not claim the tests were run; provide the appropriate command and describe the expected observable result without inventing execution output.

title: Refactor With a Clear Boundary
description: Plan and implement a focused refactor while preserving externally observable behavior.
prompt:
You are a refactoring partner working on [code]. The maintainability problem is [problem], the required behavior is described in [behavior contract], and the relevant project constraints are [constraints]. Keep the change focused on the stated problem.

Explain which dependency, duplication, naming, or control-flow issue creates the current difficulty. Propose a small transformation that improves that issue without introducing an unnecessary abstraction. Preserve public interfaces, error behavior, ordering, and side effects unless a change is explicitly required. Separate behavioral changes from structural changes, and flag any case where the existing behavior cannot be determined from the material.

Return a concise rationale, the revised code, and a summary of the important differences. Include a verification plan centered on observable behavior and the highest-risk paths. If a larger redesign might help later, describe it as a separate option rather than embedding it in the refactor. State any assumptions or missing context. The result should be easier to understand and change, with a clear argument for why behavior remains consistent.

title: Explain an Unfamiliar Code Path
description: Explain how a code path works using concrete inputs, state changes, and failure points.
prompt:
Act as a patient engineering mentor. Explain [code excerpt] to someone with [experience level]. The surrounding context is [system context], and the part I especially want to understand is [focus]. Base the explanation on the supplied code rather than assumptions about the larger project.

Start with the code's purpose and the inputs and outputs that matter. Walk through one representative execution path, describing important state changes and interactions. Explain unfamiliar language or framework features when they affect behavior. Distinguish what the code guarantees from what depends on callers, external services, or missing definitions. Do not infer hidden behavior as fact.

Return a plain-language overview, an annotated walkthrough, and a compact example with fictional values. Identify likely failure points and confusing details without turning the explanation into an unsolicited rewrite. Finish with three comprehension questions and their answers, plus any missing context needed for a complete understanding. Keep the depth appropriate to the stated experience level and make the causal sequence easy to follow.

title: Build a Correct SQL Query
description: Translate an analysis question into a SQL query with explicit grain and data assumptions.
prompt:
You are a SQL analyst helping answer [analysis question] using [database schema]. The SQL dialect is [dialect], and the business definitions are [metric definitions]. Available examples or data caveats are in [data notes].

Determine the required output grain before joining tables or aggregating. Check relationship cardinality, null handling, time boundaries, duplicate records, and the meaning of filters. Use only tables and fields present in the schema. Do not invent a column or assume a timestamp's timezone. When a business definition is incomplete, explain the assumption or ask for the exact missing detail within the output.

Return the query, a short explanation of each major step, and a description of the result columns. Include a small set of validation queries or checks that could reveal duplicated joins, missing records, or incorrect totals. Note dialect-specific behavior and any indexing considerations supported by the schema. Do not claim performance or results without execution evidence. Prefer a readable query whose correctness can be inspected over clever compression.

title: Investigate a Performance Bottleneck
description: Create an evidence-led performance investigation that narrows the bottleneck before changing code.
prompt:
Act as a performance investigation partner. Review [performance symptoms] in [system context] using [measurements and traces]. The relevant workload and limits are [workload and constraints]. Help identify what to measure next and where a change might matter.

Separate latency, throughput, resource use, and variability. Identify which observations point to a bottleneck and which merely occur at the same time. Consider the relevant request path, data size, concurrency, caching, and external dependencies without assuming any is the cause. Do not promise an improvement or invent benchmark results. Avoid broad optimization advice that cannot be tied to the evidence.

Return a ranked hypothesis table with supporting evidence, counterevidence, and a targeted check for each hypothesis. Propose a reproducible measurement plan with a baseline, representative workload, and controls for noise. Suggest the smallest plausible change for the strongest hypothesis and a way to evaluate side effects. Finish with stop conditions and missing measurements. The plan should allow the team to reject weak explanations and verify whether a change addresses the actual bottleneck.

title: Plan a Safe Data Migration
description: Draft a staged migration plan with validation, recovery, and compatibility considerations.
prompt:
You are a database migration reviewer. Plan the change described in [migration goal] for [current schema and usage]. The deployment environment is [environment], and the operational constraints are [constraints]. Use [available migration tooling] only where its capabilities are established.

Identify data transformations, application compatibility, write behavior, and dependencies that could affect the transition. Consider whether the migration can be staged and which steps are reversible. Distinguish rollback of application code from recovery of changed data. Do not assume downtime is acceptable, that a backup is valid, or that a database supports transactional schema changes without evidence.

Return a phased plan covering preparation, deployment order, backfill if needed, validation, and cleanup. For each phase, state preconditions, observable completion checks, and a recovery approach. Include representative validation queries when the schema permits. Flag destructive steps and the conditions that must be confirmed before execution. Finish with unresolved technical decisions and a rehearsal plan. The output should be reviewable before any production action and honest about operations that cannot be safely undone.

title: Build an Accessible UI Component
description: Specify and implement a UI component with clear interaction behavior and accessibility considerations.
prompt:
Act as a frontend implementation partner. Build [component] in [framework and version] for [user interaction]. Follow the design and behavior requirements in [requirements] and the existing conventions in [project context].

Define the component's states, inputs, outputs, and keyboard interaction before writing code. Use appropriate semantic elements and accessible names. Consider focus behavior, errors, loading, disabled states, and reduced motion when relevant. Avoid unnecessary dependencies or custom interaction patterns when native elements meet the requirement. If framework details or project utilities are missing, make the assumption explicit rather than inventing an import.

Return the component code, relevant styles, and a short usage example. Explain the accessibility decisions that affect how people operate the component. Include a focused manual verification checklist covering keyboard use, visible focus, screen-reader announcements where relevant, and narrow layouts. Flag any requirement that needs user testing or browser verification. Do not claim conformance or successful testing from code inspection alone. Keep the implementation small enough to understand and adapt.

title: Map Application Security Boundaries
description: Review a feature design for trust boundaries and concrete defensive controls.
prompt:
You are a defensive application security reviewer. Review [feature design] in [system architecture]. The important data and operations are [sensitive assets], and the stated constraints are [security requirements]. Focus on improving the design using the information provided.

Identify actors, entry points, trust boundaries, and places where input or authority crosses between components. Examine authentication, authorization, validation, secrets handling, logging, and abuse controls when relevant. Distinguish confirmed weaknesses from unanswered design questions. Do not provide exploitation instructions, invent an incident, or claim the system is secure after a document review. Prefer specific controls tied to a plausible failure condition.

Return a compact data-flow description, a prioritized risk table, and recommended mitigations with ownership placeholders. For each risk, state the precondition, affected asset, potential consequence, and evidence from the design. Include verification checks for the proposed controls and any tradeoffs that product or engineering must resolve. Finish with the missing information that prevents a firmer assessment. Keep the review actionable and proportional to the described feature.

title: Write Developer Setup Documentation
description: Create a reproducible setup guide from project material and mark any missing steps.
prompt:
Act as a developer documentation editor. Turn [project notes] into a setup guide for [developer audience]. The supported environment is [environment], and the first successful task should be [first task]. Use [existing commands and configuration] as the authoritative source for technical details.

Arrange the guide in the order a new developer will follow: prerequisites, configuration, installation, execution, and verification. Explain why a nonobvious step is needed. Use placeholders for secrets and avoid including actual credentials. Do not invent commands, package versions, files, or environment variables. Where a required step is missing, insert a clearly labeled question or gap instead of a plausible guess.

Return the complete guide with copyable commands only when supplied or directly supported by the material. Include expected observable outcomes without fabricating terminal output. Add a troubleshooting table for issues documented in the notes and a short reset or cleanup section where supported. Finish with unresolved documentation gaps. The guide should help a reader reach a working setup and identify the exact point where they need assistance.

title: Write a Decision Brief
description: Compare a business decision’s options and produce a concise recommendation with explicit assumptions.
prompt: Act as an operations adviser preparing a decision brief for [decision]. Use [business context] to understand the goals, constraints, and people affected. Evaluate the alternatives in [available options] against [decision criteria]. First identify missing information that could materially change the choice; then continue with clearly labeled assumptions where a provisional comparison is possible. Separate facts supplied by me from your interpretation. Do not invent costs, market data, performance claims, or stakeholder preferences. Consider implementation effort, reversibility, dependencies, and the downside of delaying the decision. Produce a one-page brief containing the decision statement, a comparison table, the strongest case against each option, and a recommended path with its reasoning. Finish with the next three actions, an owner role for each, and the evidence needed before commitment. If the evidence does not support a recommendation, state what would resolve the uncertainty.

title: Test a Business Model
description: Expose the riskiest assumptions in a business model and design affordable validation experiments.
prompt: Act as a business model analyst. Examine [business idea] for the customers described in [target customers], using [known evidence] and the limits in [test budget and time]. Map the proposed customer problem, value proposition, delivery approach, revenue mechanism, and major costs. Identify which elements are supported by evidence and which remain assumptions. Rank the assumptions by how damaging failure would be and how uncertain they are, explaining your judgment without fabricated probabilities. Design three practical experiments that could challenge the highest-risk assumptions before substantial investment. Each experiment must specify the hypothesis, participant or data source, procedure, observable signal, decision rule, and likely limitation. Use placeholder thresholds when I have not supplied a defensible benchmark. Return a compact model summary, an assumption table, and an ordered experiment plan. Conclude with what to keep, revise, or stop if each experiment fails.

title: Document a Repeatable Process
description: Turn process notes into a usable standard operating procedure with ownership and exception handling.
prompt: Act as a process documentation specialist. Convert [process notes] into a standard operating procedure for [intended users]. The procedure starts at [start trigger] and ends when [completion condition] is met. Preserve the actual sequence and responsibilities in the notes, and flag contradictions or missing steps instead of silently resolving them. Use plain language that a new team member can follow without specialist knowledge. Describe each step with its purpose, required input, responsible role, action, and observable completion check. Include handoffs, approval points, and exceptions only when supported by the source material. Where a necessary detail is missing, insert a clearly labeled confirmation item. Deliver a short overview, a numbered procedure, an exception table, and a final checklist. Finish with the five most consequential questions to answer before the procedure becomes official. Do not invent systems, service levels, policy requirements, or escalation contacts.

title: Compare Vendors Against Requirements
description: Build a transparent vendor comparison that distinguishes documented capabilities from unanswered questions.
prompt: Act as a procurement analyst evaluating [vendor options] for [business requirements]. Use only the claims, prices, and evidence contained in [vendor materials], with [evaluation priorities] guiding the comparison.
